g11-history-uh2-t1.overview: Africa was one of the great centres of ancient civilization, and along the Nile two remarkable cultures arose: ancient Egypt and the kingdom of Kush-Meroe. Both were shaped by the river and its annual flood, and both eventually fell to outside conquerors.
objectives: Analyse the major achievements of ancient Egyptian civilization
Explain how the Nile and its floodwaters from the Ethiopian highlands made Egypt possible
Describe the government, social classes and religion of ancient Egypt
Trace the rise and decline of the kingdom of Kush-Meroe
Explain the cultural and technological links between Egypt and Kush
g11-history-uh2-t1.simple: Africa was home to two of the ancient world's great civilizations: Egypt and Kush-Meroe. Both grew along the Nile. The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile', because the river's annual flood, fed from the Ethiopian highlands, left water and fertile soil for farming. About 3,100 B.C. Menes united Upper and Lower Egypt and founded a capital at Memphis. Egypt's kings, called pharaohs, ruled with absolute power, and the people built pyramids, invented hieroglyphic writing and advanced in medicine, mathematics and irrigation. To the south, Nubia and Kush shared much with Egypt, including pyramids and gods. Kush conquered Egypt and founded the 25th dynasty, later moved its capital to Meroe, and grew rich on iron and trade until Aksum destroyed it.
g11-history-uh2-t1.detailed:
Egypt, the gift of the Nile. The Greek historian Herodotus (about 484-425 B.C.) called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile', because the river made life possible in an otherwise dry land. The annual flood, much of it coming from the highlands of Ethiopia, carried water and fertile soil along the river and the delta. The Nile also gave Egypt political unity, served as a highway linking north and south, and acted as a trade route along which merchants exchanged the products of Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean. Egypt had two regions, Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the north covering the delta. About 3,100 B.C. Menes, king of Upper Egypt, united the two regions and founded the first capital at Memphis.

Three kingdoms and a long history. Scholars divide ancient Egyptian history into the Old Kingdom (c. 2,686-2,181 B.C.), the Middle Kingdom (c. 2040-1730 B.C.) and the New Kingdom (c. 1550-1080 B.C.), separated by the First and Second Intermediate periods when central authority broke down. In all there were 31 dynasties of indigenous rulers. After the New Kingdom, native rule ended with the final Persian conquest in 343 B.C. Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians in 332 B.C., and Macedonia-Greek rule lasted until Egypt became part of the Roman Empire in 30 B.C.

Government and society. The pharaoh was seen as both human and divine, held absolute power and owned and ruled all the land. During the Old Kingdom the kings ruled from Memphis through a bureaucracy, with a vizier, or chief minister, supervising departments for tax collection, farming and the all-important irrigation system, while thousands of scribes carried out orders. In the Middle and New Kingdoms the capital moved to Thebes and the country was divided into 42 provinces called nomes, each run by an appointed official called a nomarch. Society was a hierarchy: the pharaoh at the top, then government officials and religious leaders, then merchants, scribes and artisans, and at the bottom the peasants, the largest group, with slaves providing free labour and acting as the backbone of the economy.

Egyptian women. Egyptian women generally enjoyed higher status and greater independence than women elsewhere in the ancient world. Under Egyptian law a woman could inherit property, enter business deals, buy and sell goods, go to court and obtain a divorce. Women manufactured perfumes and textiles, managed farming estates and served as doctors, and they could enter the priesthood, especially in the service of the goddesses. The few women who learned to read and write were still excluded from becoming scribes or holding government jobs.

Religion, pyramids and the New Kingdom. Religion shaped Egyptian life. The people worshipped many gods and goddesses, including Amon-Re, Osiris, who was the god of the Nile and controlled the annual flood, and Isis. During the Old Kingdom pharaohs built necropolis, or cemeteries, containing majestic pyramids near Memphis; the largest, built for the pharaoh Khufu, is the Great Pyramid erected at Giza. The New Kingdom produced powerful rulers, among them Egypt's first female ruler, Queen Hatshepsut (c. 1473-1458 B.C.), who encouraged trade with the eastern Mediterranean lands and along the Red Sea coast of Africa. Her successor Thutmose III (1479-1425 B.C.) expanded Egypt to its greatest extent, conquering Palestine and Syria in the north and Kush and Nubia in the south.

Achievements and decline. The ancient Egyptians made lasting contributions in architecture, the hieroglyphic writing system, medicine, mathematics, the calendar and irrigation agriculture. After about 1100 B.C. the power of Egypt gradually declined. Invaders such as the Assyrians and the Persians conquered the Nile region, and in 332 B.C. the last Egyptian dynasty ended when the Greeks took control.

Kush-Meroe. Nubia is the geographic region that stretched from the southern boundary of Egypt southward to include present-day Sudan. Sharing the Nile with Egypt, Nubia borrowed much of Egyptian culture: art, architecture, some gods, customs and clothing, royal rituals, the hieroglyphic writing system and pyramids. Women played an important role there as queens. Kush rose to power in the 700s B.C. In 751 B.C. the Kushite king Piankhi attacked the Egyptian city of Memphis, and within about 15 years he controlled Egypt, uniting Egypt and Kush and founding Egypt's 25th dynasty. Two periods mark Kushite history, named after the capital and the king's tomb: Napata first, then Meroe. About 590 B.C. Meroe replaced Napata as capital. Meroe sat on the Nile and on trade routes from the Red Sea to the interior of Africa, with access to gold and iron. Taught by their defeat at the hands of the Assyrians in the 8th century B.C. that they needed iron weapons, the Kushites learned iron smelting. Meroe's prosperity rested on trade in ivory, slaves, skins, ostrich feathers, ebony and gold, and its power peaked between the middle of the 3rd century B.C. and the 1st century A.D. Decline began in the middle of the 1st century A.D. with the rise of the rival empire of Aksum, and in the middle of the 4th century A.D. the Aksumite king Ezana invaded, sacked and burned Meroe, ending ancient Kush.

workedExamples.problem: Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile'. Using the textbook, explain what made the river so important.
workedExamples.given: The annual flood comes from the Ethiopian highlands and leaves water and fertile soil; the river also links north and south and serves as a trade route.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: geography shapes civilization, because water, fertile soil and transport support settlement and state building.
workedExamples.substitution: Apply the idea to the Nile: the flood supports farming, the river unites north and south, and boats carry trade.
workedExamples.calculation: Each function of the river meets a basic need of an early state, namely food, communication and exchange.
workedExamples.answer: The Nile supplied water and fertile soil, made political unity possible, served as a highway, and carried trade, so Egypt depended on it.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the position of women in ancient Egypt with women in most other ancient societies.
workedExamples.given: Egyptian women could inherit property, enter business, buy and sell goods, go to court and obtain a divorce, and could serve as doctors and priests, but they could not become scribes or hold government office.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: comparison uses explicit criteria such as legal rights, economic activity and access to public office.
workedExamples.substitution: Check Egyptian women against those criteria and note where they were ahead and where they were limited.
workedExamples.calculation: Legal and economic rights were broader than elsewhere, while scribal and government careers remained closed to them.
workedExamples.answer: Egyptian women had unusually strong legal and economic rights, but were still excluded from scribal and government jobs.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Kushites learn iron smelting, and why was Meroe well placed for iron production?
workedExamples.given: The Assyrians defeated Kush in the 8th century B.C., and Meroe lay close to iron ore deposits.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: cause and effect, in which defeat creates a need and geography provides the means to meet it.
workedExamples.substitution: Link the military defeat to the need for iron weapons, and Meroe's location to its supply of iron ore.
workedExamples.calculation: The defeat created the motive, and the nearby ore deposits made production possible.
workedExamples.answer: Defeat by the Assyrians showed Kush that it needed iron weapons, and Meroe's closeness to iron ore made it an ideal centre for producing iron.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how Aksum brought the ancient kingdom of Kush to an end.
workedExamples.given: Meroe's decline began in the middle of the 1st century A.D. because of the rise of Aksum; in the middle of the 4th century A.D. King Ezana invaded and his army sacked and burned Meroe.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: states rise and fall in relation to rival powers.
workedExamples.substitution: Treat Aksum as a rival empire whose growth first weakened Meroe, then ended it by conquest.
workedExamples.calculation: Rivalry weakened Meroe over time, and a military invasion delivered the final blow.
workedExamples.answer: The rise of Aksum weakened Meroe from the middle of the 1st century A.D., and Ezana's invasion in the middle of the 4th century A.D. destroyed it.

commonMistakes: Confusing Upper Egypt with Lower Egypt: Upper Egypt lay in the south and Lower Egypt in the north, around the delta.
Thinking the pharaoh was only a political ruler, when Egyptians believed the pharaoh was also a god.
Believing the Nile mattered only for farming, when it also unified Egypt and carried trade.
Assuming Kush simply copied Egypt and achieved nothing of its own, when it produced its own art, language, writing system and gods.
Ignoring the Ethiopian link: the Nile flood came from the Ethiopian highlands and Aksum later destroyed Meroe.
Muddling the key dates: 3,100 B.C. for the unification by Menes, 332 B.C. for the Greek conquest and 30 B.C. for Egypt becoming a Roman province.
applications: Explaining to a neighbour why the annual Nile flood, fed from the Ethiopian highlands, was central to ancient Egypt.
Using the Nile example to argue why Ethiopia should protect its rivers, lakes and watersheds.
Reading a museum or textbook label about the Great Pyramid and identifying it as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu at Giza.
Tracing on a map how the Nile linked Upper and Lower Egypt with Nubia and Meroe.
Debating whether Kush was merely a copy of Egypt or a civilization with its own achievements, using evidence from the lesson.
Noting that Aksum, part of the Ethiopian past, was the power that finally ended ancient Kush.
g11-history-uh2-t1.summary: Ancient Egypt and Kush-Meroe were the two great African civilizations of the ancient world, both built along the Nile. Egypt developed a strong centralized state under pharaohs, built pyramids, invented hieroglyphic writing and advanced in medicine, mathematics and irrigation agriculture. Kush shared much of Egyptian culture, ruled Egypt during the 25th dynasty and later flourished at Meroe on iron and trade until Aksum destroyed it in the middle of the 4th century A.D.

g11-history-uh2-t2.overview: Asia was home to several of the earliest civilizations, most of them based on city-states and great river valleys. This lesson examines Mesopotamia, including Sumer, Babylon, Assyria and Persia, together with India and China.
objectives: Identify the major civilizations that flourished in Mesopotamia
Explain the positive and negative aspects of Hammurabi's code of law
Describe the origins and beliefs of Hinduism and Buddhism in India
Explain the achievements of ancient India in mathematics and science
Compare Confucianism and Legalism in ancient China
g11-history-uh2-t2.simple: Asia was the cradle of several early civilizations. In Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the Sumerians built city-states about 2900 B.C., invented cuneiform writing, and gave us 60 minutes in an hour. Babylon produced the law code of Hammurabi (1792-1750 B.C.), while the Assyrians built a great empire through conquest and the Persians organised it into provinces called satrapies. In India, the Dravidians built the Indus Valley cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa; later Hinduism and Buddhism arose there, and Indian scholars invented the decimal system and the symbol for zero. In China, the Shang and Zhou dynasties produced bronze work, a logographic script, the teachings of Confucius, and inventions such as silk, paper, printing and gunpowder.
g11-history-uh2-t2.detailed:
Mesopotamia, the land between rivers. By about 2900 B.C. civilization flourished in Sumeria, in present-day southern Iraq, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. The name Mesopotamia comes from a Greek word meaning 'between rivers'. Sumerian city-states were ruled by absolute kings called lugals, who governed as the representative of the city-state's chief god but were not themselves gods, unlike the pharaohs of Egypt. Most inhabitants were farmers; others were priests, officials, soldiers, craftsmen and traders. Because stone and good timber were scarce, no great monuments for kings were built, and archaeologists instead find mounds of structures made of mud bricks dried in the sun.

Sumerian achievements. The plough was first used in Sumeria, and the Sumerians became experts in metal working, producing bronze artifacts. Like the Egyptians they developed astronomy and mathematics, using them for a calendar, land measurement and administration, and we owe to them the ideas of 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. Between about 3200 and 2900 B.C. they developed a writing system of word pictures that grew into wedge-shaped characters called cuneiform, pressed with a hand instrument into soft clay tablets that dried in the sun. Cuneiform was a complex, non-alphabetic system, like hieroglyphics. Mesopotamian scholars made a careful study of the celestial bodies, recognised the difference between planets and fixed stars, and so laid the foundation of modern astronomy.

Babylon, Assyria and the New Babylonian Empire. Babylon was a great city on the banks of the Euphrates near present-day al-Hillah, Iraq, and its name means 'gate of the god'. Records first mention it about 2200 B.C. King Sumuabum founded a Babylonian dynasty in 1894 B.C., and the best known king of that dynasty was Hammurabi, who ruled from 1792 to 1750 B.C. and was famous for a fair code of law. The economic laws show buying, selling, lending at interest and private property, but the criminal laws were harsh and discriminatory across social classes and gender, and punishments for ordinary people were more severe and physical. Hammurabi's code became a model for later codes. The Assyrians, called the 'Romans of Asia', built the largest empire in the Middle East from the 9th century B.C. Their capital was first Ashur, named after their chief god, and later Nineveh, both on the Tigris, and their absolute king ruled as the representative of Ashur. Their army of cavalry, chariots and infantry used siege techniques and iron weapons rather than bronze. Assyria declined after the mid 7th century B.C., and in 612 B.C. Ashur and Nineveh were captured and destroyed by the Medians and Babylonians. The New Babylonian Empire began in 626 B.C. under Nabopolassar and reached its glory under Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 B.C.), when walls almost 26 metres thick were built and the famous Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the ziggurat later known as the Tower of Babel stood there. In 539 B.C. Persian invaders captured Babylon.

Persia and Zoroastrianism. Ancient Persia included parts of what is now Iran and Afghanistan. The founder of the Persian Empire was Cyrus the Great (557-530 B.C.), and his successors extended it into the largest of all ancient empires. The emperor was an absolute ruler who governed as the representative of the Persian god Ahura Mazda, and the empire was divided into provinces called satrapies, each under an official called a satrap. Persians taught their sons to ride horses, shoot bows and speak the truth, and to lie or to be in debt was considered disgraceful. Peasants used irrigation and underground tunnels to grow wheat, barley, oats and vegetables, caravans carried goods across Persia to the Mediterranean Sea, and a gold currency called darics, first issued by Darius I, was used all over the empire. The prophet Zoroaster, or Zarathustra, lived in the 6th century B.C. and introduced Zoroastrianism, teaching two opposing principles, good represented by Ahura Mazda and evil by Ahriman. Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire in 331 B.C.

India: the Indus Valley and its religions. The first Indian civilization began in the Indus Valley about 2500 B.C. and reached its height about 1500 B.C. It was started by the Dravidians, who were indigenous to northern India. Archaeologists have found two major cities, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, with streets laid out in a rectangular pattern, good water supply and drainage systems, and buildings of bricks baked in furnaces, all suggesting some kind of urban planning. Scholars explain the destruction of this civilization by environmental degradation through deforestation, epidemic disease such as malaria, changes in the course of the Indus River and climatic change. Afterwards Indo-Aryan peoples moved from northern India and Persia into the interior, conquered the Dravidians and established the civilized states of ancient and medieval India, while southern India remained largely Dravidian. Hinduism developed from the beliefs of the early Indo-Aryans; one basic common idea is that mankind is condemned to a cycle of rebirths, and salvation can be won, for example, by giving up the pleasures of the material world and seeking spiritual enlightenment under the guidance of a guru. Buddhism emerged from Hinduism as a reform movement, founded by Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563-483 B.C.), who taught the 'middle way' that avoids the extremes of asceticism on one side and materialism on the other, and it spread outside India to South East Asia, China and Japan.

Indian science and mathematics. Indian physicians advanced surgery and introduced the use of herbs to cure diseases. Hindu scientists made it possible for craftsmen to tan leather, dye cloth and produce soap, cement, glass and finely hardened steel. Their greatest contribution was in mathematics: the numerals we call Arabic (1, 2, 3 and so on) were first used in India and were later taken over and developed by the Arabs, and the Indians also introduced the decimal system and the symbol for zero.

China: from Shang to Qin. China's earliest centres of civilization were in the northern Huang-He valley. The first dynasty was the Shang (c. 1700-1122 B.C.), a highly developed society governed by a hereditary class of aristocrats, whose achievements included magnificent bronze vessels, horse-drawn war chariots and a system of writing. The earliest Chinese script used pictographs, drawings of the objects they represented, which became more simplified as the script developed; the language has about 50,000 characters and the writing system is logographic. About 1122 B.C. the Zhou people of western China overthrew the Shang and ruled until 256 B.C., and the last part of their rule is called the 'warring states period' (403-221 B.C.). Confucius (551-479 B.C.), whose real name was Kong Qiu or K'ung Fu-Tzu, meaning Great Master Kong, was the most influential philosopher in Chinese history. His ideas, called Confucianism, stress the development of moral character and responsibility, and his sayings were recorded by his disciples in the Analects; Confucianism became the official and dominant ideology of China from about 100 B.C. until the revolution of 1911. He taught five cardinal human relationships: ruler to subject, father to son, husband to wife, elder brother to younger brother, and friend to friend, and summarised ethics as 'Do not do to others what you do not want done to you'. Mencius (372-289 B.C.) believed people are born good and stressed the natural compassion of the heart. In 221 B.C. the Qin state defeated its rivals and established China's first empire under the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, who believed in Legalism, a philosophy emphasising authority, efficient administration and strict laws. A combination of legalistic administration and Confucian moral values helped Chinese empires endure for more than 2000 years. The ancient Chinese were also great inventors: they first used coal, were the first to produce porcelain, invented the wheelbarrow and varnish, started the silk industry, made paper from cotton about 150 A.D., first developed printing, and used gunpowder as early as 600 A.D.

workedExamples.problem: Was the code of Hammurabi fair? Evaluate it using evidence from the textbook.
workedExamples.given: The economic laws show buying, selling, lending at interest and private property, while the criminal laws were harsh and discriminatory across social classes and gender, and punishments for ordinary people were more severe and physical.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: evaluation weighs strengths and weaknesses against a standard such as equal treatment before the law.
workedExamples.substitution: Note which parts protected property and trade fairly and which parts punished people unequally according to class and gender.
workedExamples.calculation: The code gave clear rules and protected economic life, but it failed the standard of equal treatment because it punished the poor more harshly.
workedExamples.answer: It was partly fair, because it regulated trade and property, but it was also harsh and discriminatory, and it became a model for later codes.

workedExamples.problem: Why was civilization able to develop in river valleys such as those of the Tigris and Euphrates, and later the Indus?
workedExamples.given: The Tigris and Euphrates encircle Mesopotamia; the Indus Valley supported the cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: geography shapes civilization, because water and fertile soil support farming, surplus food and settled cities.
workedExamples.substitution: Apply the concept to each valley: rivers supply water and soil, and the surplus feeds officials, priests and craftsmen.
workedExamples.calculation: In each case a river valley provided the food surplus and transport that made cities, writing and government possible.
workedExamples.answer: River valleys provided water, fertile soil and transport, so farming produced the surplus food that cities and states need.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the idea of the 'middle way' in Buddhism and why the religion spread beyond India.
workedExamples.given: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563-483 B.C.) and taught a middle way between asceticism and materialism; it spread to South East Asia, China and Japan.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: religions spread when their teachings answer widely felt needs and are carried by trade, travel and contact.
workedExamples.substitution: Show what the middle way offered: it avoided extremes that most people could not follow, and it promised a path to salvation.
workedExamples.calculation: Because it was a reform movement within Hinduism that moderated extreme practices, it attracted followers and travelled along the same routes as trade.
workedExamples.answer: The middle way avoided both extreme self-denial and extreme luxury, and its clear teaching helped Buddhism spread to South East Asia, China and Japan.

Treating Confucianism as a religion, when it was basically a secular philosophy based on human reason.

g11-history-uh2-t3.overview: The earliest civilization in Europe arose in Greece, not along a single river valley but in independent city-states, one of which experimented with direct democracy. Rome then built a vast empire whose law, roads, language and peace shaped the modern world.
objectives: Describe the form of government in the Greek city-states, especially Athens
Distinguish direct democracy from representative democracy
Explain the philosophical, historical and medical achievements of the ancient Greeks
Describe the social hierarchy, government and military expansion of Rome
Explain the Pax Romana and the decline and division of the Roman Empire
g11-history-uh2-t3.simple: Ancient Greece and Rome were the great civilizations of Europe. The Greeks developed independent city-states called poleis; Athens grew largest, practised a direct democracy in which adult citizens, but not women or slaves, voted in the Assembly, and produced philosophers such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and the doctor Hippocrates. Constant wars between city-states, especially the Peloponnesian War (431-404 B.C.), weakened Greece, and Macedonia under Philip II and Alexander the Great conquered it. Rome, founded by tradition in 753 B.C., became a republic in 509 B.C. and then a vast empire. Its law, roads, aqueducts and the Pax Romana left a lasting mark, though the West collapsed in 476 A.D. while the East survived until 1453.
g11-history-uh2-t3.detailed:
Greek city-states and the polis. The ancient Greeks developed the earliest civilization in Europe, sometime around 2500 B.C. Unlike most ancient civilizations that thrived along river valleys, Greek civilization flourished in different independent city-states. A city-state is a small, independent country consisting of a single city whose government exercised full sovereignty over itself and all territories within its borders, and the single city was the centre of political, economic and cultural life. The Greek term for city-states is polis, derived from the Acropolis of the 5th century, which served as the centre of Athenian government. The form of government was oligarchy, rule by a few powerful people, though during the 5th century B.C. some city-states began to practise democracy. Athens and Sparta were the best known city-states. Athens was the largest in size and population, with between 25,000 and 40,000 people in the 5th century B.C.; it had good olive oil and wine but little fertile land for grain, so it imported grain from the coastal areas of the northern Black Sea, and it was known for its strong navy.

Athenian democracy. Athens introduced the principle of direct democracy, in which all adult citizens, except women and slaves, took part in decision making. Citizens could attend, speak and vote in the general meeting called the Assembly, which passed laws, determined government policies and elected Athenian generals. This was direct democracy, because the citizens decided matters themselves rather than sending representatives to decide for them. The limits were severe: women and slaves were excluded, so most people in Athens had no vote at all.

Greek culture and learning. During the 5th century B.C. Athens became the centre of Greek culture, and philosophy originated there. Socrates (470-399 B.C.), Plato (427-347 B.C.) and Aristotle (384-322 B.C.) are considered the most important Greek philosophers, and at the centre of Greek philosophy was the pursuit of truth or reality by the power of human reason. The Greeks pioneered in medicine, physics, biology and mathematics, and Greek architects, sculptors and painters built the Parthenon, a temple on the Acropolis. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote many masterpieces of drama. Herodotus (484-425 B.C.), called the Father of History, and Thucydides (460-400 B.C.) established proper historiography. Modern medicine sees its founder in the Greek doctor Hippocrates (460-357 B.C.), and in many medical schools today doctors take the Hippocratic Oath on graduation, an oath he first applied to his pupils.

War, Macedonia and the Hellenistic Age. The glorious days of Athens ended with the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War (431-404 B.C.), a series of wars among the city-states in which Athens was defeated by Sparta. Their power then declined considerably, paving the way for outside attack. Macedonia, a country north of Greece, was becoming stronger as the Greek city-states grew weaker. In 353 B.C. Philip II, king of Macedonia, set out to conquer Greece, and the independence of the Greek city-states ended in 338 B.C. when he defeated them. On his death his son and successor, Alexander the Great (336-323 B.C.), led a Greek and Macedonian army and conquered the entire Persian Empire, spreading Greek ideas and language in Egypt and the Near East. After his death in 323 B.C. the empire was divided among his generals. The period from the death of Alexander to the Roman conquest of Greece in 30 B.C. is known as the Hellenistic Age, when Greeks came into contact with outside peoples and their classic culture blended with cultures from Asia and Africa.

Rome: from village to republic. Tradition says that about 753 B.C. twin brothers named Romulus and Remus established a settlement on the Palatine Hill, the centre-most of the Seven Hills of Rome and the first nucleus of the Roman Empire. Since 1000 B.C. the Latins, the first settlers, had lived on this hilly area. From the 7th century B.C. the Etruscans, who had lived north of the Palatine hills, controlled Rome; they are remembered for finely constructed roads, temples and public buildings, they promoted trade and introduced the idea of the citizen assembly, and under them Rome grew from a village of farmers and shepherds into a prosperous city. The people drove out the Etruscans, overthrew the monarchy and established the Roman Republic in 509 B.C. The Senate was the most powerful government body; it conducted foreign policy, passed decrees and handled the treasury.

Roman society and expansion. Roman social structure was hierarchical. Citizens were divided into three classes: the patricians, or nobles, the Equites, and the plebeians, or common people. The patricians were members of Rome's oldest and richest families and held all the important political positions, and all senators were patricians. The Equites were the richest of the non-nobles, owning land and sometimes working as businessmen. The plebeians were small farmers, craftsmen, shopkeepers and labourers who also cultivated the latifundia, the large landed estates of the upper classes. The system still allowed mobility, so skilled slaves, Greeks and others might work as managers, clerks, accountants and teachers. Slaves were often harshly treated and their revolts were rare because they were crushed in the bud; one unsuccessful revolt was led by Spartacus from 73 to 71 B.C., and its participants were punished by crucifixion. Slaves were seldom freed, through a system called manumission, and the motive was more economic than humanitarian, since it was given to skilled slaves to encourage good work. Rome slowly gained control of the Italian peninsula, offering protection and the privileges of Roman citizenship to conquered cities while they supplied soldiers in return. By 270 B.C. Rome controlled most of Italy, and colonial expansion made it a mighty empire during the 2nd and 1st centuries B.C. Rome then came into conflict with Carthage, a sea power and trading centre on the coast of northern Africa, and the two fought for mastery of the Mediterranean in three struggles called the Punic Wars, lasting from 204 to 146 B.C. After Carthage was defeated, Rome controlled the Mediterranean coasts of Spain and Africa; it then conquered the Hellenistic monarchies, including Egypt, so that by the end of the 1st century B.C. it controlled all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea.

From Augustus to the fall of the West. Conflicts among leaders caused upheaval in the last 100 years of the Republic. Julius Caesar (100-44 B.C.) became sole ruler, and in 44 B.C. a group of senators who feared his growing power assassinated him. Power then was divided between Octavian, Caesar's adopted son, and Mark Antony, Caesar's friend, who sought the support of Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt (47-30 B.C.). In 31 B.C. Octavian defeated their forces and made Egypt a Roman province, and in 27 B.C. he became the first Roman emperor, taking the title Augustus. He preferred to be called princeps, meaning first citizen. His reign began the Pax Romana, or Roman peace, which lasted about 200 years and brought order, flourishing trade and growth in art and literature. The Romans did not match the cultural and intellectual achievements of the Greeks, but they produced fine Latin literature and excelled in war, the arts of government and law; Roman law became the base of many legal systems in Western Europe and Latin America. They are remembered for their civil and military roads and their aqueducts, and for architecture such as the Roman Forum, the Temple of Venus and Rome and the Roman Colosseum. We owe the modern Latin alphabet to the Romans, who adapted it from the Etruscans and the Greeks. In 395 A.D. the empire was split into the West Roman Empire, centred at Rome, and the East Roman or Byzantine Empire, centred at Constantinople, now Istanbul. The West then declined and shrank: Spain, Gaul, now France, and North Africa were controlled by Germanic peoples such as the Vandals and Visigoths; in 410 A.D. the Visigoths looted Rome; and in 476 A.D. the West Roman Empire formally collapsed. The East Roman Empire survived until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople.

workedExamples.problem: Was Athenian democracy truly democratic? Evaluate it using the evidence in the lesson.
workedExamples.given: All adult citizens could attend, speak and vote in the Assembly and hold office, but women and slaves were excluded, and the population of Athens was between 25,000 and 40,000.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: evaluation measures a system against a principle, here the principle that all people should have a voice.
workedExamples.substitution: Compare who was included, namely adult male citizens, with who was excluded, namely women and slaves.
workedExamples.calculation: Because a large part of the population had no vote, the system fails the principle of equal participation even though it involved citizens directly.
workedExamples.answer: It was a real but limited democracy: direct for adult male citizens, but undemocratic for women and slaves.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how the Peloponnesian War helped bring about the end of Greek independence.
workedExamples.given: The Peloponnesian War lasted from 431 to 404 B.C. and Athens was defeated by Sparta; afterwards the power of the city-states declined and Macedonia grew stronger.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: cause and effect, in which internal conflict weakens a group and invites outside conquest.
workedExamples.substitution: Link the exhausting war to the weakened city-states and the rising strength of Macedonia.
workedExamples.calculation: The war drained the city-states, so Philip II could defeat them in 338 B.C. and end their independence.
workedExamples.answer: The war weakened all the city-states, leaving them unable to resist Macedonia, which ended their independence in 338 B.C.

workedExamples.problem: Why are Roman law and Roman roads regarded as important contributions to later civilizations?
workedExamples.given: Roman law became the base of many legal systems in Western Europe and Latin America, and the Romans built civil and military roads to link the empire as well as aqueducts to carry water to towns.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: contributions are judged by how long and how widely they continue to shape later societies.
workedExamples.substitution: Ask where each contribution can still be found: law in modern legal codes, roads in the transport systems that hold states together.
workedExamples.calculation: Because both the law and the roads were adopted far beyond Rome and lasted centuries, they count as major contributions.
workedExamples.answer: They shaped later legal systems and linked distant regions, so they influenced many societies long after Rome.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the main reasons for the collapse of the West Roman Empire in 476 A.D.
workedExamples.given: In 395 A.D. the empire was split into West and East; Germanic peoples such as the Vandals and Visigoths took over provinces; the Visigoths looted Rome in 410 A.D.; and in 476 A.D. the West Roman Empire formally collapsed.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: states decline through a combination of internal division and external pressure.
workedExamples.substitution: Treat the split as internal weakening and the Germanic invasions as external pressure.
workedExamples.calculation: Division reduced the West's strength while invasions removed its provinces and finally its central authority.
workedExamples.answer: The division of 395 A.D. weakened the West, Germanic invasions took its provinces, and in 476 A.D. its central authority collapsed.

commonMistakes: Thinking ancient Greek civilization grew along one great river valley, when it actually grew in independent city-states.
Believing Athenian democracy gave everyone the vote, when women and slaves were excluded.
Confusing direct democracy, where citizens decide themselves, with representative democracy, where they elect others to decide.
Mixing up the Greek writers: Herodotus is the Father of History, Thucydides also wrote history, and Hippocrates founded modern medicine.
Saying the Roman Republic began in 753 B.C.; the traditional founding of Rome was 753 B.C., but the Republic began in 509 B.C.
Believing the whole Roman Empire fell in 476 A.D., when only the West collapsed and the East survived until 1453.
applications: Comparing direct democracy in Athens with the representative system used in Ethiopia today, where citizens elect representatives.
Debating why a system that excludes women and slaves should not be called fully democratic.
Recognising the Hippocratic Oath when reading about how Ethiopian doctors and health workers are trained today.
Using the Pax Romana to discuss how peace and security allow trade and development to flourish.
Noting that features of Ethiopian school and government life, such as written law and public roads, have deep roots in the ancient world.
Reading a news report about the European Union and recalling how Rome once united the lands around the Mediterranean.
g11-history-uh2-t3.summary: Greece and Rome were the great civilizations of ancient Europe. The Greeks lived in independent city-states, and Athens practised a direct democracy limited to adult male citizens while producing major achievements in philosophy, history, medicine, art and architecture. Greek independence ended with the Peloponnesian War and the rise of Macedonia under Philip II and Alexander the Great. Rome moved from a village to a republic in 509 B.C. and then to a vast empire, leaving a legacy of law, roads, aqueducts and the Pax Romana; its western half fell in 476 A.D. while the eastern half survived until 1453.

g11-history-uh2-t4.overview: Mesoamerica and the Andes were home to three of the world's great civilizations: the Maya, the Aztec and the Inca. They raised great cities, pyramid temples and road systems, and their achievements in farming, medicine and mathematics were remarkable.
objectives: Explain how people first reached the Americas and how farming supported early cities
Describe the farming methods, social hierarchy and religion of the Maya
Explain the achievements and tribute system of the Aztec empire
Describe the government, religion and technology of the Inca empire
Compare the major achievements of the Maya, Aztec and Inca civilizations
g11-history-uh2-t4.simple: The Maya, Aztec and Inca built great civilizations in Latin America. Mesoamerica, made up of Mexico and Central America, was the first major centre. The Maya, the earliest to build large cities, flourished from about 250 A.D. in the Classic Period, with powerful city-states such as Tikal and Calakmul, a 365-day solar calendar and a numbering system that included zero, though their cities never formed one empire. The Aztec entered the valley of Mexico in the 1200s and founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, collecting tribute from conquered states and building floating gardens on the lake. In the Andes, the Inca founded their empire about 1450, ruled from Cuzco by an emperor believed to be the son of the sun god Inti, and built stone walls, terraces and roads without cement. All three civilizations were later overwhelmed by Spanish conquest.
g11-history-uh2-t4.detailed:
The Americas and Mesoamerica. The Americas include two continents, North America and South America. Within these regions lies Mesoamerica, made up of Mexico and Central America, a major spot where culture and civilization first thrived in that part of the world. Most scholars believe that between 12,000 and 10,000 years ago people first arrived in the Americas from Siberia and Alaska through a land bridge now known as the Bering Strait. As elsewhere, the greatest adaptation came when people learned to domesticate plants and animals, a change that took place slowly between about 8500 B.C. and 2000 B.C. In Mesoamerica Neolithic people cultivated beans, sweet potatoes, pepper, tomatoes, squash and maize, the Native American name for corn, while people in South America cultivated maize and cassava and domesticated llamas and other animals valued for their wool. By 3000 B.C. in parts of South America and 1500 B.C. in parts of Mesoamerica, farmers had settled in villages, and some of these villages eventually grew into the great early cities of the Americas.

The Maya: cities and farming. The Maya were the earliest people to build large cities, by 300 B.C., in what is now Guatemala. By about 250 A.D. the Maya Golden Age, also known as the Classic Period, began, with city-states flourishing from the Yucatan Peninsula in southern Mexico through much of Central America. Before they developed large population centres the Maya lived scattered, and they developed two farming methods that allowed them to thrive in the tropical environment: they cleared the forest in order to plant on it, and along the banks of rivers they built raised fields to lift crops above the annual floodwaters. This produced enough maize and other crops to support rapidly growing cities. The Maya cities never formed an empire; there were many city-states of which the most powerful were Tikal and Calakmul. Conflicts and wars were common among them, but they maintained regular contact through trade, which generated a great deal of wealth, in everyday goods such as honey, salt and cotton and in prized items such as feathers, precious stones and jaguar hides.

Maya society, religion and learning. Maya society showed a distinct hierarchy. Each city had its own ruler, usually male, though records and carvings show that women occasionally governed on their own or in the name of young sons. Nobles held military leadership, managed public works, collected taxes and enforced laws, while scribes, painters and sculptors were also highly respected. Merchants formed a middle class, and the wealthiest merchants were certainly nobles. The majority of the Maya were farmers who grew maize, beans and squash as well as fruit trees, cotton and flowers, and there were slaves in some cities, captured in war. The cultural life of the Maya included impressive advances in learning and the arts and a complex polytheistic religion. Their cities are known today for towering temples and palaces built from stone, with temples resting on pyramid-shaped platforms where priests performed rites and sacrifices, and some temples served as burial places for rulers, nobles and priests. They developed a hieroglyphic writing system which scholars did not interpret until recent decades. Because priests needed to measure time accurately for ceremonies, many became expert mathematicians and astronomers: they developed an accurate 365-day solar calendar and invented a numbering system that included the concept of zero. About 900 A.D. the Maya stopped building cities and their civilization began to decline, though no one knows exactly why; suggestions include overpopulation, disease or drought, or peasant revolts against the priests and nobles. By the time the Spanish arrived in the 1500s, the Maya mostly lived in farming villages.

The Aztec: rise and the capital. As Maya civilization weakened, other peoples such as the Zapotec and Toltec fought for control of southern Mexico and built large cities and pyramid temples. Then, in the 1200s A.D., the Aztecs pushed their way into the valley of Mexico. They were a warlike people, and in 1325 A.D. they established a capital named Tenochtitlan. They conquered neighbouring towns and cities and forced the conquered people to pay tribute in the form of food, feathers, gold, cotton and slaves. The Aztec empire reached its height under Montezuma II (1592-1521), who collected tribute from 371 states; the emperor had supreme power and appointed officials to administer justice and regulate trade. Like the Romans, the Aztecs built roads to link distant outposts to the capital, and soldiers were stationed at strategic spots along the roads to protect travellers such as merchants. In the 1500s Tenochtitlan was a bustling city with about 100,000 inhabitants. As the city grew they expanded their island capital: engineers built walkways, roads made of packed earth, to connect the island to the mainland, while farmers filled in parts of the lake and dug drainage canals to create more farmland and anchored reed baskets filled with earth in the shallow lake, planting crops in the baskets to make floating gardens. A huge pyramid temple and the emperor's palace dominated Tenochtitlan, and the palace served as a storehouse for tribute and housed the royal family, thousands of servants and officials, a zoo and a library of history books and accounting records.

Aztec knowledge and religion. Like the Romans, the Aztecs adopted ideas from the peoples they conquered, and Aztec priests used the knowledge of astronomy and mathematics. Like the Maya, they developed a 365-day solar calendar. Aztec priests used herbs and other medicines to treat fevers and wounds; their physicians could set broken bones in place and treat dental cavities, and they prescribed steam baths as cures for various illnesses, a therapy still in use today. The Aztecs worshipped many gods, including the gods of corn, rain, sun and war, and their calendar was like a religious text that told people which month was sacred to each god and goddess. A large class of priests performed ceremonies meant to ensure the goodwill of the gods, and Aztec religious practices included human sacrifices offered to the sun god, with prisoners of war used as the victims.

The Inca: empire and government. In about 1450 A.D. the Inca founded the last great empire in the Andes region of Latin America, stretching from what is today Ecuador through Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. The Incas developed an efficient system to govern their huge empire. The emperor was an absolute ruler; he divided the empire into provinces and appointed nobles to govern them, and governors were responsible for taking a census so that people could be taxed. The government was sensitive to the aged, the sick and the poor. Like many other peoples of the time, the Incas worshipped gods and looked to their priests to tell them the will of the gods. They believed that the emperor was the son of the sun god Inti, the chief god of the land, and as a result they called themselves the 'children of the sun'. In Cuzco, the capital of the empire, priests and priestesses performed outdoor ceremonies in the Great Sun Temple.

Inca technology and the end of the empire. The Incas developed advanced technology in many areas. They diverted streams and rivers to mine for gold, which artisans then made into fine ornaments, and they invented a system of measurement. Inca priests had enough medical knowledge to perform successful brain surgery, and they learned to treat victims of malaria with quinine, whose value Europeans did not understand until the 1800s. The Inca dragged huge stone blocks to build magnificent temples and palaces and shaped the stones to fit perfectly without applying cement between them; during the violent earthquakes that occasionally rock the Andes, Inca stone walls sway but do not tumble down. They also built roads that linked distant provinces to Cuzco, and they used their building skills for farming by constructing terraces, or flat areas, on steep mountainsides to create land that could be planted. The Inca had no system of writing, but certain people memorised their history and taught it to the next generation, and the government recorded census data, the size of harvests and historical events. In the early 1500s the Inca Empire reached its greatest size, but when Spanish soldiers arrived on the coast of Peru in 1532, internal power rivalry had significantly weakened the empire, which paved the way for easy conquest.

workedExamples.problem: How did the Maya produce enough food to support their growing cities in a tropical environment?
workedExamples.given: The Maya cleared forest in order to plant on it, and along the banks of rivers they built raised fields to lift crops above the annual floodwaters, producing enough maize and other crops to support rapidly growing cities.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: adaptation, in which a society changes its methods to suit its environment.
workedExamples.substitution: Identify the environmental problems, namely dense forest and seasonal flooding, and match each farming method to the problem it solves.
workedExamples.calculation: Clearing made land available, and raised fields protected crops from the flood, so together they produced the needed surplus.
workedExamples.answer: By clearing forest and building raised fields above the floodwaters, the Maya produced the food surplus that large cities required.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why historians are not certain about the decline of Maya civilization about 900 A.D.
workedExamples.given: The Maya stopped building cities and their civilization declined, and scholars suggest overpopulation, disease or drought, or peasant revolts against the priests and nobles, but no one knows for certain.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: historians rely on evidence, and where evidence is incomplete they present competing hypotheses rather than one certain answer.
workedExamples.substitution: List the hypotheses offered and note that each fits some of the evidence without proving the case completely.
workedExamples.calculation: Because several explanations remain possible and none is fully proven, historians keep the question open.
workedExamples.answer: The evidence does not settle the question, so historians offer several possible causes, including overpopulation, disease, drought and peasant revolt.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the achievements of the Aztec and the Inca empires.
workedExamples.given: The Aztec built roads, floating gardens, a 365-day calendar and medical treatments, while the Inca built terraces, earthquake-resistant stone walls, roads, a measurement system and performed brain surgery.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: comparison uses shared categories such as farming, building, government, medicine and learning.
workedExamples.substitution: Place the achievements of each people side by side under those categories.
workedExamples.calculation: Both excelled in building roads and in medicine and farming, but the Inca are distinguished by stonework without cement and by brain surgery, while the Aztec are distinguished by floating gardens and tribute records.
workedExamples.answer: Both built roads and advanced medicine and farming, but the Aztec are known for floating gardens and tribute, and the Inca for cementless stonework, terraces and brain surgery.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Inca empire fall so easily to the Spanish in 1532?
workedExamples.given: In the early 1500s the Inca Empire reached its greatest size, but internal power rivalry had significantly weakened it when Spanish soldiers arrived on the coast of Peru in 1532.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: internal division makes a state vulnerable to outside conquest.
workedExamples.substitution: Link the power struggle among the Inca to the timing of the Spanish arrival.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the empire was divided by rivalry at the very moment of invasion, it could not unite to resist.
workedExamples.answer: Internal power rivalry had weakened the empire, so the Spanish faced a divided state, which paved the way for easy conquest.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Maya formed one large empire, when they had many city-states and never made a single empire.

Mixing up capitals: Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital, while Cuzco was the Inca capital.
Believing the Inca had a writing system, when in fact certain people memorised history and the government kept records in other ways.
Thinking the Aztec and Inca empires fell only because of Spanish weapons, ignoring the role of internal rivalry and disunity.

g11-history-uh2-t4.summary: Three great civilizations arose in Latin America. The Maya were the earliest to build large cities, flourished during the Classic Period from about 250 A.D., and developed hieroglyphic writing, an accurate 365-day calendar and the concept of zero, though their city-states never formed an empire. The Aztec founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, built a tribute empire and used floating gardens, roads and medicine. The Inca founded an empire about 1450, ruled from Cuzco by an emperor believed to be the son of the sun god Inti, and were masters of stone building, terraces and road making. All three were eventually overcome by Spanish conquest.

g11-history-uh2-t5.overview: Christianity arose among the Jews of Roman-controlled Judea and grew from a small Jewish following into the official religion of the Roman Empire. Its early story includes persecution, the growth of church organisation, and the councils that defined its doctrine.
objectives: Describe the position of the Jews under Roman rule in Judea
Explain the life and teaching of Jesus as recorded in the Gospels
Trace the growth of the early Church and its organisation, including the five patriarchates
Explain the decisions of the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople
Describe how Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire and later split into West and East
g11-history-uh2-t5.simple: Christianity began among the Jews of Judea, which the Romans conquered in 63 B.C. The Jews believed in one God and were allowed religious freedom, but some zealots called for revolt, and in 70 A.D. the Romans crushed a rebellion and destroyed the Jewish temple. Christianity arose among the followers of a Jew named Jesus, whose life is known mainly from the four Gospels. Jesus taught love of God and neighbour and the importance of forgiveness; at about 30 A.D. he was arrested, tried and condemned to death by crucifixion. The early Christians organised themselves under bishops, archbishops and patriarchs, with five patriarchates, and Church councils at Nicaea in 325 A.D. and Constantinople in 385 A.D. defined the doctrine of the Holy Trinity. Though Christians were persecuted for refusing to sacrifice to the emperor, persecution ended in 313 A.D. when Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, and Theodosius I later made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire.
g11-history-uh2-t5.detailed:
Judea under Roman rule. In 63 B.C. the Romans had conquered Judea, the southern part of Palestine where most Jews of the time lived. The Jews had long believed in a monotheistic religion, Judaism. To avoid violating the Jewish belief in one God, the Romans allowed them religious freedom as they did elsewhere in the vast empire. While most Jews were reluctantly willing to live under Roman rule, others called zealots were not, and they called on Jews to revolt against Rome. Some believed that a messiah, an anointed king sent by God, would soon appear to lead their people to freedom, but the rebellion did not last long: in 70 A.D. the Romans crushed the revolt and then destroyed the Jewish temple, which ushered in a gloomy period of Jewish enslavement and dispersal. Over the centuries since the destruction of Jerusalem, Jewish religious teachers called rabbis extended and preserved the Jewish law, and Judaism has survived.

Jesus and the Gospels. As turmoil engulfed the Jews in Palestine, a new religion, Christianity, arose among them. It began among the followers of a Jew named Jesus. Almost all the information we have about the life of Jesus comes from the Gospel, the first four books of the New Testament of the Christian Bible, which early Christians attributed to four followers of Jesus named St. Matthew, St. Mark, St. Luke and St. John. According to Jesus, a person's major duties were 'to love the Lord your God with all your heart' and 'to love your neighbor as yourself', and he also emphasised the importance of forgiveness. Some Jews welcomed Jesus to Jerusalem, while others regarded him as a dangerous troublemaker; the Jewish priests in particular felt that he was challenging their leadership, and to the Roman authorities he was seen as a revolutionary who might lead the Jews in a rebellion against Roman rule. At about 30 A.D. he was arrested, tried and condemned to death by crucifixion.

The growth of the early Church. The first Christians were Jews in Palestine and Syria, but soon many gentiles, that is non-Jews, were converted to Christianity. The number of gentile Christians gradually exceeded that of the Jewish Christians, and in the end Jewish Christians were either assimilated into gentile Christianity or went back to Judaism and ceased to be Christian. The head of each local Christian community was the bishop. In time archbishops appeared who had spiritual authority over the bishops, other clergy and laity of a large area. Then the rank of patriarch emerged: a patriarch had spiritual authority over the archbishops, bishops, other clergy and laity of very large regions called patriarchates. There were five patriarchates: Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Constantinople and Jerusalem. Earlier, the Patriarch of Rome, also called the Pope, was claiming leadership over the other patriarchs. From about the middle of the third century onwards, monasteries where monks and nuns lived in separate communities were established; monks who lived together had a leader called an abbot, while those who lived alone were called hermits.

Heresies and the Church councils. Doctrines which were rejected and condemned by the Church were called heresies, and the followers of these doctrines were called heretics. The Church's doctrines were approved by Church councils, which were meetings of the patriarchs, archbishops and bishops of the Church. The Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. established the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, and this doctrine was confirmed by the Council of Constantinople in 385 A.D. The doctrine of the Holy Trinity says that one God exists in three persons, God the Father, God the Son, who is Jesus, and God the Holy Spirit, and that all these persons are equal. The council condemned Arianism, a belief that rejected the divine nature of Jesus.

Persecution and the Edict of Milan. The early Christians faced serious persecution from the Roman rulers because Christians would not make sacrifices in honour of the emperor, and refusal to sacrifice was considered political disloyalty by the Roman government. Nevertheless the number of Christians and the Christian churches increased from time to time in the midst of severe persecution. With the conversion of Constantine, the Roman, to Christianity, the persecution of Christians came to an end in 313 A.D. The emperor then issued the Edict of Milan, which guaranteed freedom of worship to all inhabitants of the Roman Empire.

The official religion and the split of the Church. Later, the Emperor Theodosius I, who reigned from 379 to 395, declared Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire and repressed the practice of other faiths. Christianity had a Western and an Eastern Church since 395 A.D. The centre of the Western Church was in Rome under the leadership of the Pope, and the Eastern centre was in Constantinople under the Patriarch. In 1054 A.D. Christianity was split into the Catholic West and the Orthodox East.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Roman rulers persecute the early Christians?
workedExamples.given: Christians would not make sacrifices in honour of the emperor, and refusal to sacrifice was considered political disloyalty by the Roman government.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: persecution often has a political as well as a religious cause.
workedExamples.substitution: Separate the religious belief, namely worship of one God, from the political charge, namely refusal to honour the emperor.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the refusal was read as disloyalty to the state rather than merely a private belief, the Romans punished it.
workedExamples.answer: The Romans saw the Christian refusal to sacrifice to the emperor as political disloyalty, so they persecuted them.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the doctrine of the Holy Trinity using the decisions of the Church councils.
workedExamples.given: The Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. established the doctrine and the Council of Constantinople in 385 A.D. confirmed it; the doctrine states that one God exists in three persons who are equal.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: doctrine is defined by collective decisions of the Church in councils, not by single individuals.
workedExamples.substitution: Identify what the first council established and what the second council confirmed, and what Arianism denied.
workedExamples.calculation: Nicaea set out the three persons of the one God, Constantinople confirmed this, and Arianism was condemned for rejecting the divine nature of Jesus.
workedExamples.answer: The councils taught that one God exists in three equal persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and condemned Arianism.

workedExamples.problem: What did the Edict of Milan change, and why does it matter?
workedExamples.given: Persecution ended in 313 A.D. with Constantine's conversion, the emperor issued the Edict of Milan, and it guaranteed freedom of worship to all inhabitants of the Roman Empire.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a turning point is an event that changes the direction of later events.
workedExamples.substitution: Compare what came before, namely persecution, with what came after, namely legal freedom of worship.
workedExamples.calculation: Because Christians could worship freely and churches multiplied, the edict marks the turning point towards Christianity becoming the official religion.
workedExamples.answer: It ended persecution and guaranteed freedom of worship, which allowed Christianity to grow until it later became the official religion.

workedExamples.problem: Christianity grew even though Christians were persecuted. Explain how this was possible.
workedExamples.given: The number of Christians and the Christian churches increased from time to time in the midst of severe persecution, and the faith spread from Jewish Christians to gentiles across the empire.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: ideas spread through networks of people and roads even when they face opposition.
workedExamples.substitution: Consider the message that attracted gentiles and the conditions, such as travel and trade, that allowed it to spread.
workedExamples.calculation: Persecution could not stop the growth because the teaching appealed widely and the empire's travel and trading networks carried it from community to community.
workedExamples.answer: Persecution did not stop the spread: the teaching attracted many gentiles, and travel and trade networks carried it across the empire.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Romans forced all their subjects to abandon their own religion, when they allowed the Jews religious freedom.
Confusing the five patriarchates with the later division of the Church into West and East.
Mixing up the councils: Nicaea in 325 A.D. established the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, and Constantinople in 385 A.D. confirmed it.
Believing persecution ended at the birth of Christianity; it continued until Constantine and the Edict of Milan in 313 A.D.
Assuming the Western and Eastern Churches split in 395 A.D., when they began then and split only in 1054 A.D.
Equating heresy with modern crime, when it meant a doctrine rejected and condemned by the Church.
applications: Comparing the respect for councils and tradition in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church with the early Church councils.
Explaining how the 365-day calendar used in Ethiopia and much of the Christian world comes from the ancient world.
Discussing why freedom of worship, guaranteed by the Edict of Milan, still matters for religious tolerance in Ethiopia today.
Tracing on a map the five patriarchates and noting that Alexandria and Jerusalem lie in Africa and the Middle East.
Reflecting on how the teaching to love your neighbour as yourself shapes moral behaviour in daily life.
Using historical thinking to separate what the Gospels say from what other sources say about early Christianity.

The early Church grew under bishops, archbishops and patriarchs, with five patriarchates, and the councils of Nicaea in 325 A.D. and Constantinople in 385 A.D. defined the Holy Trinity and condemned Arianism. Persecution ended with Constantine and the Edict of Milan in 313 A.D., Theodosius I made Christianity the official religion of the empire, and in 1054 A.D. the Church split into the Catholic West and the Orthodox East.
